questions.q: Why does the lesson say a maturity score like 'we went from Initial to Advanced on Identity' is close to meaningless to a non-technical executive on its own?
options: Executives are never shown any numbers at all in a progress update
Maturity stages are confidential and cannot be shared outside the security team
The stage names change meaning between different CISA reports
An executive cares about whether the organization's exposure and spending are producing results, not what the stage labels mean technically
questions.explain: A CFO or board member cares about two things in the moment: is exposure to a costly incident going down, and is the money spent on the program producing that result — a stage label alone doesn't answer either.

questions.q: What are the three parts of the translation pattern the lesson recommends applying to every technical finding?
options: Risk reduction, business impact, and trend over time
Vendor name, product version, and purchase date
Pillar name, maturity stage, and audit date
Root cause, remediation ticket number, and closure date
questions.explain: Every finding should answer: what risk went down in plain terms, what the business impact would have been without the change, and whether the trend is moving the right direction and how fast.

questions.q: In the worked translation table, how does 'standing domain admin accounts dropped from 200 to 3' get reframed for an executive audience?
options: By removing the number entirely and only naming the tool (PAM) that was purchased
By stating that if an attacker steals one employee's credentials, the number of systems they could immediately control dropped by over 98%, with most access now expiring in 30 minutes
By reporting that domain admin accounts are no longer allowed to exist under any circumstances
By stating that the organization is now fully compliant with all applicable regulations
questions.explain: The translation keeps the real number, drops the acronym (PAM/JIT), and states the counterfactual risk in a sentence a non-technical reader can repeat back accurately.

questions.q: In the one-slide structure for a recurring executive update, why does the lesson recommend showing a trend line across several reporting periods instead of a single snapshot number?
options: Trend lines are required by the CISA ZTMM for all executive reporting
A snapshot number is always inaccurate compared to a trend line
A single snapshot invites the question 'is that good?' — a trend line shows the direction and pace of change without anyone needing to ask
Trend lines take less time to prepare than a single number
questions.explain: Showing the same outcome metric across the last several reporting periods makes the direction and pace of improvement visible at a glance, rather than leaving the audience to guess whether one number is good or bad.

questions.q: Why does the one-slide structure include a sentence naming the biggest remaining exposure honestly, rather than only reporting good news?
options: Naming a gap is a formal compliance requirement under Executive Order 14028
It removes the need to report any trend data at all
Boards legally require a documented risk statement in every security presentation
A program that only ever reports good news loses credibility the first time something goes wrong, so naming the real gap yourself builds the trust that keeps the budget funded
questions.explain: Naming the biggest remaining exposure before an auditor or an incident surfaces it builds credibility and keeps the reporting trustworthy over the long run, rather than setting up a credibility collapse later.
